source: Brier (1950) Verification of forecasts expressed in terms of probability
finding: Proposed the squared-error score for probability forecasts of weather. Could not be opened (HTTP 403, NOAA mirror also failed). Facts here come from Gneiting and Raftery and Wikipedia, which I did open.
numbers: For m classes the score is the sum of (indicator - p_j)^2. For a binary event it is (f - o)^2.
limits: Source text not read. Treat details as second-hand.
agent_relevance: Base score for the S9 class record: one number per resolved probability, 0 best, 0.25 for always saying 50%.

source: Gneiting & Raftery (2007) Strictly proper scoring rules, prediction, and estimation
finding: A scoring rule is proper if the forecaster's best expected score comes from reporting their true belief. Strictly proper if that is the only best report. The Brier (quadratic) score is strictly proper. Gives the Savage representation: every proper rule comes from a convex function G. Brier is the case with a uniform mixing measure over cost ratios.
numbers: Table 1: Brier S(p,1) = -(1-p)^2, S(p,0) = -p^2, uniform measure. Log score: log p and log(1-p), density (c(1-c))^-1. Spherical and zero-one also tabulated.
quote: In prediction problems, proper scoring rules encourage the forecaster to make careful assessments and to be honest.
limits: Zero-one score is not strictly proper. Log score is unbounded. Choice among proper rules matters when losses are asymmetric.
agent_relevance: Only proper rules should score the agent's probabilities. Plain accuracy is not proper and rewards rounding to 0 or 1.

source: Gneiting & Raftery (2007) section 2.3 skill scores and hedging
finding: Skill scores built from a proper rule (such as the Brier skill score, 1 - BS/BS_ref) are generally not proper. Murphy (1973) showed the Brier skill score is only asymptotically proper: gains from hedging vanish as the number of independent forecasts grows. A claim by Mason (2004) of exact propriety rests on unjustified approximations.
numbers: No sample sizes. The statement is asymptotic.
limits: Asymptotic, so with a small class record the skill score can be gamed.
agent_relevance: Log raw Brier per class. Report skill against a stated reference only as a derived view, never as the quantity the agent maximises.

source: Gneiting & Raftery (2007) Bregman divergence and entropy view
finding: Each proper rule has an expected score function G(p) = S(p,p) (an entropy) and a loss d(P,Q) (a Bregman divergence). For Brier the divergence is squared Euclidean distance. The loss is zero only if the forecast equals the true distribution.
numbers: Brier entropy term is 1 - sum p_j^2. The log score gives Shannon entropy and KL divergence.
limits: Theory for a known true distribution; real forecasts are scored on single outcomes.
agent_relevance: Explains why Brier splits into an uncertainty part (task difficulty) and an error part (our fault). Log them separately.

source: Wikipedia: Brier score (worked example and decomposition)
finding: Worked example: forecast 0.70 for rain. Score 0.09 if it rains, 0.49 if not. Forecast 0.30 and rain gives 0.49. The page lists the three-part split into uncertainty, reliability and resolution, and cites Murphy (1973), J. Appl. Meteorol. 12(4):595-600, and a bias-corrected decomposition by Ferro and Fricker (2012, Q. J. R. Meteorol. Soc. 138:1954-1960). States the Brier skill score is not strictly proper.
quote: Even if the Brier score is a strictly proper scoring rule, the BSS is not strictly proper
limits: Secondary source. I could not open Murphy 1973 or Ferro and Fricker 2012.
agent_relevance: Sanity test for our logger: a 0.7 forecast must log 0.09 or 0.49.

source: Murphy (1973) A new vector partition of the probability score
finding: Splits the mean Brier score into reliability (calibration error), resolution (how far conditional hit rates differ from the base rate) and uncertainty (base-rate variance). Not opened (HTTP 403). The form BS = REL - RES + UNC is as given in the secondary sources I read.
numbers: UNC = obar(1 - obar). Exact only when forecasts take a finite set of values and are grouped by value.
limits: Source text not read. Dimitriadis et al. say it fails to be exact for continuous forecasts.
agent_relevance: S9 can store the three terms per class: separates bad calibration (fixable by recalibration) from weak discrimination (not fixable that way).

source: Brocker (2009) Reliability, sufficiency, and the decomposition of proper scores
finding: Extends the Brier decomposition to any strictly proper score for finite-valued targets: expected score = uncertainty - resolution + reliability. Resolution and reliability each improve the score. The resolution term acts like the variance of the calibrated forecast. Links to DeGroot and Fienberg sufficiency and refinement.
numbers: Equation (13) in the paper; symbols are garbled in the text extraction, so no formula copied.
quote: This term reduces to the standard variance of ... in case of the Brier score.
limits: Finite number of outcomes; the Brier case has the simple closed form.
agent_relevance: Log reliability and resolution for any proper score we pick. Recalibrating a forecast (making it reliable) cannot hurt the score.

source: Dimitriadis, Gneiting & Jordan (2021) Stable reliability diagrams (CORP)
finding: Binned reliability diagrams are unstable because bin choices are ad hoc. CORP uses isotonic regression (pool-adjacent-violators) to give a bin-free reliability diagram and a Brier decomposition into MCB (miscalibration), DSC (discrimination) and UNC. It generalises to any proper score and is exact. Notes Murphy's decomposition is exact for discrete forecasts but not continuous ones.
numbers: Table 2, precipitation forecasts, S / MCB / DSC / UNC: ENS .266/.066/.044/.244; EPC .234/.022/.032/.244; EMOS .232/.018/.030/.244; Logistic .206/.017/.056/.244 (n = 86 forecast values).
quote: Murphy's decomposition is exact in the discrete case, but fails to be exact under continuous forecasts
limits: Weather example; simulations use n = 1024.
agent_relevance: Use PAV/CORP rather than ten fixed bins when the class record is small or probabilities are continuous. Report MCB, DSC and UNC.

source: Dimitriadis et al. (2021) bin-count sensitivity
finding: With binning and counting, estimated miscalibration depends on the number of bins, and estimates are biased. In their simulations CORP had the smallest mean squared error at every sample size tested.
numbers: Binned approach: squared bias decays like m(n)^-2 while variance grows with bin count. CORP lowest MSE over all sample sizes.
limits: Simulation conditions chosen by the authors.
agent_relevance: Do not read much into ECE from a few dozen resolved items. The estimate is noisy.

source: Guo, Pleiss, Sun & Weinberger (2017) On calibration of modern neural networks
finding: Modern deep networks are overconfident. More depth and width raise ECE even as error falls. Temperature scaling (one parameter fitted on a validation set by minimising NLL) fixes most of it and leaves accuracy unchanged. Defines ECE (weighted mean gap between accuracy and confidence over M bins) and MCE (largest bin gap).
numbers: ECE (15 bins), uncalibrated -> temperature scaling: CIFAR-100 ResNet-110 16.53% -> 1.26%; ResNet-110 (SD) 12.67% -> 0.96%; CIFAR-10 ResNet-110 4.6% -> 0.83%; Birds ResNet-50 9.19% -> 1.85%; 20 News DAN-3 8.02% -> 4.11%; Reuters DAN-3 0.85% -> 0.91%. ECE typically 4 to 10% before calibration.
quote: temperature scaling outperforms the vector and matrix Scaling
limits: Reuters is the one dataset not helped (already under 1%). 20 News gain is modest. ECE depends on bin scheme. Vision and text classifiers, not LLMs.
agent_relevance: Cheap post-hoc fix: fit one temperature or one Platt-style map on the class record. Needs held-out resolved items and does not fix discrimination.

source: Kadavath et al. (2022) Language models (mostly) know what they know
finding: Large pretrained models are well calibrated on multiple choice when options are shown in A/B/C format, and calibration improves with model size and few-shot prompting. They also do well on True/False. Replacing an option with 'None of the above' harms performance and calibration. A model can be trained to predict P(IK), the chance it knows the answer, and P(True) for its own samples.
numbers: ECE with 10 equal-count bins; chance Brier on binary choice 0.25. Tasks: BIG-Bench multiple choice, TruthfulQA, QuALITY, LogiQA, MMLU, up to 52B parameters.
quote: models are well-calibrated (in this format) even for somewhat adversarial datasets like TruthfulQA
limits: Format dependent. P(IK) generalises poorly to new tasks: on Lambada it gave uniformly low scores and calibration was terrible; training on all 4 tasks fixed it.
agent_relevance: Token-level confidence over shown options is a usable signal. A learned self-assessment does not transfer to new task types without data.

source: Kadavath et al. (2022) RLHF effect
finding: Helpful-and-harmless RLHF policies look very miscalibrated. A single temperature adjustment (T = 2.5, same for all evaluations) largely fixes it on MMLU, MMLU True/False and TruthfulQA (52B, 5-shot).
numbers: T = 2.5 for all tasks. Evidence is calibration curves (Figure 9), no ECE table in that section.
quote: Of course more intensive RL training might distort calibration in ways that cannot be remedied in this way
limits: Quick experiment, one RLHF recipe, curve reading only.
agent_relevance: Our agent will be a tuned chat model. Expect probabilities that are off and plan a temperature or Platt fit on the class record.

source: Kadavath et al. (2022) metrics: ECE, AUROC, Brier
finding: ECE is the mean absolute difference between probabilities and frequencies over bins; they also use RMS error. They add AUROC and Brier because a model that always says one value can have good ECE. Brier combines discrimination and calibration.
numbers: 10 equal-count bins; chance Brier 0.25 for binary tasks; chance AUROC 0.5.
quote: Brier scores combine the discriminative power of self-evaluation with calibration
limits: They report cases with a tradeoff between best AUROC and best calibration.
agent_relevance: Pair a calibration metric with a discrimination metric, or use Brier alone, which includes both.

source: Tian et al. (2023) Just ask for calibration: gpt-3.5-turbo
finding: For RLHF chat models, the probability the model states in words is better calibrated than its token probabilities. Asking for top-k answers each with a probability helps more. Chain-of-thought did not improve verbalized calibration. Abstract: ECE cut by a relative 50% for ChatGPT, GPT-4 and Claude 2 across three datasets.
numbers: gpt-3.5-turbo ECE, label prob vs verbalized 1-stage: TriviaQA 0.140 vs 0.068 (top-1) and 0.050 (top-2); SciQ 0.256 vs 0.234 (top-1) and 0.065 (top-4); TruthfulQA 0.451 vs 0.389 (top-1) and 0.203 (top-4).
quote: verbalized probabilities are often better-calibrated than the model's conditional probabilities
limits: TruthfulQA ECE stays 0.2 to 0.4 and AUC is near or below 0.5. ECE-t and Brier use temperature fit on a 20% split.
agent_relevance: Ask the agent for a stated probability per candidate answer, then calibrate it afterwards.

source: Tian et al. (2023) Just ask for calibration: GPT-4
finding: GPT-4 verbalized probabilities are again better calibrated than its label probabilities, even after temperature scaling. Discrimination is not better.
numbers: GPT-4 ECE, label prob vs verbalized 1-stage: TriviaQA 0.078 vs 0.024 (top-1); SciQ 0.219 vs 0.201 (top-1) and 0.056 (top-4); TruthfulQA 0.445 vs 0.350 (top-1) and 0.198 (top-4). AUC on TriviaQA 0.950 label vs 0.937 verbalized.
limits: Verbalized ECE sometimes gets worse after temperature scaling (TriviaQA 0.024 -> 0.038). Gain is in calibration, not AUC.
agent_relevance: Verbalized confidence fixes the calibration term, not the resolution term. Rely on checks for resolution.

source: Xiong et al. (2024) Can LLMs express their uncertainty? (ICLR)
finding: Benchmark of black-box confidence on 5 LLMs and 8 tasks. Verbalized confidence is overconfident, mostly 80 to 100% in multiples of 5. Calibration and failure prediction improve with model size but stay far from ideal. Sampling several answers and measuring agreement helps failure prediction most.
numbers: Vanilla verbalized: GPT-3, GPT-3.5, Vicuna average ECE above 0.377. GPT-4 average AUROC 62.7% (random 50%). About 22.2% AUROC gain from GPT-3 to GPT-4. GSM8K with 5 samples and consistency: AUROC 54.8% -> 92.7%. GPT-4 GSM8K accuracy 93.6%, ECE 0.064 by saying 100%. Best aggregation ECE as low as 0.028. White-box vs black-box AUROC 0.605 vs 0.522 as read from the abstract.
quote: LLMs, when verbalizing their confidence, tend to be overconfident, potentially imitating human patterns of expressing confidence.
limits: Human-style prompts help less for stronger models. No method wins everywhere. All fail on professional-knowledge tasks.
agent_relevance: Agreement across samples adds resolution, but G4 says same-model samples are correlated. Treat as a hint, then calibrate. A low ECE can come from the base rate alone, so report AUROC next to it.

source: Kapoor et al. (2024) LLMs must be taught to know what they don't know
finding: Prompting alone does not give good calibration. Fine-tuning with LoRA on about a thousand graded correct and incorrect answers gives better uncertainty (ECE and AUROC) than baselines. Calibration does not improve out of the box as the base model improves. One model can estimate another model's uncertainty. A user study shows the estimates help people decide when to rely on the model.
numbers: Abstract: a thousand graded examples are sufficient to outperform baselines. ECE is the main metric. I did not extract the results tables.
quote: prompting on its own is insufficient to achieve good calibration
limits: Results tables not read in detail. Needs weights (LoRA), so not usable on a closed API.
agent_relevance: Supports keeping a graded record: about a thousand items is the order of data needed to learn a calibrator.

source: Halawi, Zhang, Yueh-Han, Steinhardt (2024) Approaching human-level forecasting with LMs
finding: A retrieval-augmented LM system forecasts binary questions after the model cutoff and nears the crowd on Brier score: .179 vs crowd .149 (accuracy 71.5% vs 77.0%). Random is .250. Plain base models score about .208 to .268 depending on model and prompt.
numbers: Test set 914 questions (table lists 3,762 / 840 / 914 questions by split). Base models, two prompt settings: GPT-4-1106 .208 / .209; Llama-2-13B .226 / .268; Claude-2.1 .220 / .215; Gemini-Pro .243 / .230; Mistral-8x7B .238 / .238; trimmed-mean ensemble .208 / .224.
quote: On average, the system nears the crowd aggregate of competitive forecasters, and in some settings surpasses it.
limits: Wins only in subsets (next line). Brier averaged across retrieval dates. Test questions published after model cutoffs.
agent_relevance: Plain prompting is about .21 to .24, near the .25 coin flip; a scaffold reaches .179. A target for the class record.

source: Halawi et al. (2024) where the system wins and loses
finding: The system beats the crowd when the crowd is unsure (crowd forecast .3 to .7): Brier .199 vs .246. It loses when the crowd is near 0 or 1, because the model hedges: 7% higher accuracy there but Brier worse by .04. Authors suspect safety training causes the hedging. Under three joint conditions it scores .240 vs crowd .247.
numbers: Crowd .3 to .7 only: ours .238, crowd .240, 51% of forecasts. 5+ articles: ours .175, crowd .143, 84% of forecasts. All three conditions: ours .240, crowd aggregate .247, 22% of forecasts, 43% of questions.
limits: Subsets were chosen after seeing validation behaviour; coverage falls to 22% of forecasts.
agent_relevance: Sharpness gap: the model will not commit to 2% or 98%. A recalibration that pushes extremes could gain Brier, but must be checked on held-out items.

source: Halawi et al. (2024) base model versus pipeline
finding: Base GPT-4-1106 without the pipeline scores .206. One ablated version of the system scores .186, which is .007 worse than the full .179. The best score of any model in the baseline evaluation was .208.
numbers: Base-only .206; ablated system .186; full system .179; baseline best .208; crowd .146 to .149.
limits: Which component was ablated is not recorded in my notes.
agent_relevance: The scaffold adds roughly .03 Brier over plain prompting. Our equal-token test (G7) can use Brier on resolved items.

source: Schoenegger & Park (2023) LLM prediction capabilities in a real-world tournament
finding: GPT-4 entered a Metaculus tournament (July to October 2023, 843 participants). It did not beat the 50% baseline and was much worse than the crowd. The idea that it hugs 50% was not supported. A weighted average of GPT-4 and the crowd (.467/.533) beat the random baseline.
numbers: GPT-4 mean Brier .20 (SD .18); human crowd median .07 (SD .08); baseline .25. GPT-4 vs .25: t(22) = -1.23, p = .23. Crowd vs .25: t(22) = -10.69, p < .001. Blend .13 (SD .09), t(22) = -5.91, p < .001. N = 23 binary questions.
limits: Tiny N. One model, one prompt, no retrieval.
agent_relevance: Without evidence retrieval the LLM is near a coin flip in Brier terms. A bad Brier here is not from midpoint hugging, so use reliability vs resolution to find the cause.

source: Schoenegger et al. (2024) Wisdom of the silicon crowd
finding: The median of 12 LLM forecasts on 31 binary questions beat the 0.25 baseline and was not statistically different from 925 human forecasters. Models showed an acquiescence effect: mean forecasts above 50% though outcomes were about even. Giving GPT-4 and Claude 2 the human median raised accuracy by 17 to 28%.
numbers: LLM crowd Brier .20 (SD .12) vs .25: t(30) = -2.35, p = .026. Human crowd .19 (SD .19). LLM vs human t(60) = 0.19, p = .850. Equivalence bound Cohen d = 0.5 (0.081 Brier): p = .017 and .040. Study 2: Brier .22 (SD .19) -> .15 (SD .14), p < .001. Human mean forecast 57.35 (SD 20.93).
limits: 31 questions only. Equivalence bounds are wide. After correction the first p-value became 0.039.
agent_relevance: Aggregation helps, but gains came from different models; same-model samples are correlated (G4). Check mean forecast against the base rate for yes-bias.

source: Karger et al. (2025) ForecastBench
finding: A dynamic benchmark of 1,000 questions about unresolved events. On a 200-question subset, superforecasters (Brier .076) beat the public (.096) and the best LLM (GPT-4o, .130). The superforecaster to GPT-4o gap (.054) is larger than the GPT-4o to GPT-4 gap (.026).
numbers: N = 200 of 1,000 questions. Superforecasters .076, public .096, GPT-4o .130. Text also gives Claude 3.5 Sonnet .122 as top LLM in a 200-item comparison.
quote: expert forecasters outperform the top-performing LLM (p-value < 0.001)
limits: Leaderboard moves; I did not check later versions. Mix includes auto-generated questions.
agent_relevance: A moving external yardstick. The human gap is about .05 Brier at that time.

source: Zou et al. (2022) Autocast: forecasting future world events
finding: Early dataset of tournament questions with a dated news corpus. Best retrieval-augmented T5 model gets 65% accuracy on binary forecasts vs 92% for the human crowd. Calibration error: the biggest FiD Static model 40% vs 8% for the crowd; giving it crowd forecasts cut it to 17%.
numbers: Adaptive-binning calibration error with 50 samples per bin: FiD Static 40%, human crowd 8%, FiD Temporal 17%.
limits: Pre-ChatGPT models. Calibration error here is ECE-like with different binning, so not comparable to later work.
agent_relevance: Shows the 2022 calibration gap to humans. Later systems (Halawi 2024) closed much of it.

source: Paleka et al. (2024) Consistency checks for language model forecasters
finding: Instant test for forecasters: ask logically related questions (negation, conditionals) and measure arbitrage profit or a frequentist violation score. Violation scores correlate with later Brier scores, so inconsistency predicts bad Brier before outcomes resolve. Also releases a consistency benchmark that resolves in 2028.
numbers: Correlation of the frequentist violation score with average Brier 0.85 (Figure 3a, scraped questions); the arbitrage metric panel shows correlation 0.4. Forecasters with Brier worse than 0.25 were excluded.
quote: if a forecasting AI illogically predicts that both the Democratic and Republican parties have 60% probability
limits: Few forecasters per plot; worse-than-chance forecasters excluded; correlation only.
agent_relevance: A cheap internal check with no outcome needed: ask the negation and see whether p + p' is 1. Fits G5 and gives S9 a signal before resolution.

source: Steyvers et al. (2025) What LLMs know and what people think they know
finding: Users trust LLM answers more than the model's own confidence warrants (calibration gap) and are worse than the model at telling right from wrong (discrimination gap). Longer explanations raise user confidence without raising accuracy. Matching explanation wording to the model's real confidence narrows both gaps.
numbers: Model AUC .751 (GPT-3.5) and .746 (PaLM2) on multiple choice, .781 (GPT-4o) on short answer; participants AUC about .59 to .60 on default explanations; mean participant AUC .54 (long) and .57 (short) in Experiments 2a to 2c. User ECE .104 to .291 across conditions.
limits: Human participants, trivia-style questions.
agent_relevance: If people read the agent output, state its probability in plain text. Length hides uncertainty (verbosity bias, G5).
